units.title: Types of Epilepsy and Generalised Tonic-Clonic Seizure (GTCS)
units.sec: Types of Epilepsy and Generalised Tonic-Clonic Seizure (GTCS) · p113
units.guide: Epilepsy is divided into generalised, partial and childhood types. Under generalised come generalised tonic-clonic seizure (GTCS), myoclonic seizure (m.s., whose commonest subtype is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, JME) and absence seizure (AS); the childhood syndromes are Lennox Gastaut syndrome (LGS) and Dravet syndrome (DS). In GTCS a T-type Ca2+ channel spontaneously generates action potentials, thalamo-cortical reciprocal firing follows, Na+ channels propagate the action potential and the spinal cord depolarises; the features are generalised muscle contraction, teeth clenching, tongue bite with blood from the mouth, and involuntary urination and defecation.

units.title: Myoclonic Seizure (m.s.)
units.guide: Myoclonic seizures occur during the morning and are characterised by twitching of the finger. They are worsened by two antiepileptic drugs - phenytoin and carbamazepine - and their commonest subtype is juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.

units.title: Absence Seizure and Partial Seizure
units.sec: Absence Seizure and Partial Seizure · p114
units.guide: Absence seizure also begins with spontaneous T-type Ca2+ channel activity and then involves Na+ channels. Typical absence seizure (most common) has no motor symptoms but behavioural abnormality with blank stare and surrounding cutoff, and its EEG shows a 3 Hz spike; atypical absence has behavioural changes plus change in muscle tone. Partial seizure, when it generalises, is treated like GTCS. Space occupying lesions (neurocysticercosis, brain tumour, gliosis from trauma or stroke) in the cortex irritate cortical neurons, generate action potentials through Na+ channels that travel to the spinal cord and cause localised depolarisation with localised muscle contraction.

units.title: Childhood Epileptic Syndromes
units.guide: Lennox Gastaut syndrome features resistant seizures and mental retardation; its treatment follows the mnemonic 'very low response to child' - valproate (DOC), lamotrigine (second), rufinamide (third), topiramate, and clobazam/cannabinoids reserved for drop attacks. Dravet syndrome has resistant seizures and is treated with ketogenic diet, valproate (DOC), clonazepam (second) and stiripentol (third). Treatment is continued to a minimum one year seizure-free interval, except in JME, stroke-induced seizure and sleep related hypermotor epilepsy (SHE), where treatment is lifelong.

units.title: Classification of Antiepileptic Drugs
units.guide: Antiepileptic drugs are classified by mechanism: Na+ channel blockers include phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, eslicarbazepine, lamotrigine, topiramate, zonisamide, lacosamide and rufinamide; Ca2+ channel blockers are valproic acid and ethosuximide (DOC in typical absence seizure); other groups are the K+ channel blockers, drugs decreasing glutamate effect, drugs increasing GABA effect and miscellaneous agents.

units.title: Valproic Acid
units.guide: Valproic acid is a Ca2+ channel blocker with the mechanism mnemonic 'H/o GTCS': it is a histone deacetylase blocker that stops neuronal proliferation, inhibits GABA transaminase so GABA rises, blocks T-type Ca2+ channels and blocks sodium channels. It is used in GTCS, m.s. and atypical absence, and is DOC in rapid cyclers, rheumatic chorea, LGS and DS. Its side effects follow the mnemonic Tab VALPROIC: tremor (epilepsy), maximum teratogenicity (bipolar disorder), vomiting, alopecia, liver toxicity (contraindicated below 2 years), pancreatitis, obesity and increased NH3 with hepatotoxicity, for which L-carnitine is the antidote.

units.title: Phenytoin (and Fosphenytoin)
units.guide: Phenytoin (diphenyl hydantoin) is used orally for GTCS and PS and intravenously for status epilepticus, with purple glove syndrome as a side effect of the IV route. Its side effects follow the mnemonic HYDANTOIN: hirsutism, hyperplastic gum, hyperglycemia, lymphadenopathy resembling Hodgkin lymphoma, and (as acute toxicity) diplopia, ataxia and nystagmus; it is teratogenic (facial cleft) and causes osteomalacia (treat with vitamin D and vitamin K), increased bleeding in newborns (give injectable vitamin K after birth) and neutropenia/anemia from folic acid depletion. Fosphenytoin is water soluble with less toxicity and is preferred over phenytoin.

units.title: Carbamazepine
units.guide: Carbamazepine is used in GTCS, PS (where it was the older DOC) and SHE. It is DOC in trigeminal neuralgia and in Rolandic epilepsy, which occurs in childhood during sleep or after awakening and is treated for 1-2 years. Its side effects are hyponatremia with SIADH (a delayed effect, most common in the elderly), hypersensitivity with eosinophilia, aplastic anemia, agranulocytosis and Stevens Johnson syndrome, plus ataxia and diplopia/blurred vision.

units.title: Lamotrigine and Topiramate
units.guide: Lamotrigine inhibits glutamate release and blocks Na+/Ca2+ channels, with an additional DHFR/5HT3 blocking action; it is used in GTCS, m.s., PS, the depressive phase of bipolar disorder and LGS. Its side effect is Stevens Johnson syndrome, so the drug must be started gradually, and it is contraindicated in acute mania where a bolus dose is needed. Topiramate acts through GPCR-mediated increased GABAA release, decreased glutamate release, potassium channel opening, Ca2+/carbonic anhydrase inhibition and resting Na channel blockade; it shares the uses of lamotrigine and is additionally used for obesity with phentermine (an anorexic agent) and for migraine prophylaxis. Its side effects are renal stones, metabolic acidosis, weight loss and angle closure glaucoma.

units.title: Other Na+ Channel Blockers: Oxcarbazepine, Zonisamide, Lacosamide and Rufinamide
units.sec: Other Na+ Channel Blockers: Oxcarbazepine, Zonisamide, Lacosamide and Rufinamide · p117
units.guide: Oxcarbazepine and eslicarbazepine are prodrugs with less hypersensitivity but more hyponatremia, so they should be avoided in the elderly. Zonisamide causes renal stones, lacosamide increases suicidal tendencies and rufinamide is used in LGS. The page notes drugs associated with SJS and HLA: carbamazepine with HLA B1502, abacavir with HLA B5701 and allopurinol with HLA B5801.
